transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, what brings me in is that I’m just losing hours of my day to rechecking things. It's... it's stuff like my dressing supplies, the door locks, and even work stuff, like file dimensions and my revision notes. I just don’t feel allowed to move on to the next thing until I’ve gone through the exact same routine enough times. I basically have to keep checking until the anxiety finally drops, and it's just taking up way too much of my time.
Are you checking these things because you're afraid something bad will happen if you don't?

Yeah, that's exactly it. Even after I know I’ve cleaned the wound area perfectly, or I've already reviewed a CAD file for work, a thought just keeps cutting in. It tells me that I missed one tiny thing, and because of that, it’s going to turn into a bad infection, or... or a design mistake that ends up hurting someone. I know I did it right the first time, but I just can’t reason the thought away.
Do you also feel a strong need to arrange things in a specific order or symmetry?

No, not really. I mean... I keep my workspace pretty organized, but I don't get that same anxious feeling about things being perfectly lined up or symmetrical. If a pen is out of place or something isn't in an exact order, it doesn't really bother me. It doesn't make me feel like something bad is going to happen. It's really just the checking that I get stuck on.
Do you experience any intrusive thoughts or images that are disturbing or unpleasant to you?

Not really, no. I mean... aside from the thoughts I just mentioned, about the infection or someone getting hurt from a CAD mistake. Those are definitely unpleasant. But I don't have, like, random disturbing images popping into my head or anything else like that, if that's what you mean. It's pretty much just tied directly to those specific mistakes I'm afraid of making.
Are your repetitive checkings primarily to prevent something specific from happening, like an infection or a design mistake, or are they more about trying to feel 'just right' or relieved?

I think it's mostly about getting that relief, getting the anxiety to go down. That's actually what brings me in here... I'm losing hours to rechecking things. It's my dressing supplies, door locks, file dimensions, revision notes. I just... I don't feel allowed to move on to whatever I need to do next until I've gone through the same routine enough times. I just have to keep checking until the anxiety finally drops.
Is your goal in repeating these checks to make sure something bad doesn't happen, or is it to feel like you've done everything correctly?

I guess it's a little of both. It starts because I want to make sure I've done everything correctly so a mistake doesn't happen. But then... like I was just saying, it turns into this trap where I end up losing hours of my day to it. 

Whether it's my revision notes at work or the door locks at home, even if I logically know I did it right the first time, I just don't feel allowed to stop. I have to keep going through the routine enough times until that anxious feeling finally goes away, and only then do I feel like I have permission to move on.
Is the relief you feel after repeating these checks more about reducing your overall anxiety level or about feeling safer from the specific harms you mentioned?

I think it's mostly about reducing the overall anxiety level. Like I said before, that's the main reason I'm here. I'm losing hours every day to just rechecking things—my dressing supplies, the door locks, the file dimensions and revision notes at work. I know I'm worried about the specific harms, but in the moment, I just don't feel allowed to move on to the next thing until I've gone through the checking routine enough times. I just keep doing it until that heavy anxiety finally drops.
Do you feel like you're trying to achieve a sense of completeness or perfection when you repeat these checks, or is it strictly about preventing those specific bad outcomes?

I wouldn't really call it perfection. It's more like... needing to finish the routine so I feel complete, I guess. I know I keep repeating myself here, but that's really what it comes down to and why I made this appointment. 

I'm losing so many hours rechecking my dressing supplies, the door locks, and all my file dimensions and revision notes at work. I just literally don't feel allowed to move on to the next task. I have to go through that same checking routine enough times until the anxiety finally drops. So it's less about making it perfect, and more about just doing it until my brain gives me permission to stop.
Are any of your checking behaviors related to concerns about germs, contamination, or getting sick?

No, not really. I mean, I don't have any issues with germs or worrying about getting sick. It's strictly just the stuff I mentioned—the locks, my dressing supplies, and the files at work. Contamination just isn't something I really think about or feel the need to check.
Do you feel like you have to repeat these checks because you're afraid of making a mistake, or because you need to feel in control of the situation?

I don't think it's really about being in control, and it's not exactly about making a mistake, either. I mean, I guess I don't want to make a mistake at work with the files, but it's really just what I was saying before. I just have to do it until it feels right. If I don't check the locks or the supplies or the files enough times, I just get stuck. It's not about control, it's just... I have to do it until the anxiety lets up and my brain lets me move on.
Do you think you would still feel the need to repeat these checks if someone you trusted told you that everything was done correctly?

I'm not really sure. I haven't... I haven't really been in a situation where someone was there to tell me that while I was doing it. 

But honestly, I think I probably would still feel the need to check. Because it's not really about whether it's actually correct logically, you know? It's about my brain giving me that feeling that it's done. Even if someone I completely trust told me the door was locked or my file dimensions were right, I feel like I'd still be stuck until I went through the routine and felt it for myself. But yeah, I don't know for sure since it hasn't really come up.
Do you feel like your checking behaviors have to be performed in a very specific way, or that there's a certain 'right' way to do them?

Yeah, it definitely has to be a specific way. It's... well, it's a routine. That's really the main thing that brings me in here, honestly. I'm losing hours to rechecking these things—the door locks, my dressing supplies, the file dimensions and revision notes at work. 

I just don't feel allowed to move on to whatever I need to do next until I've gone through that exact same routine enough times. I have to keep doing it that specific way until the anxiety finally drops. If I mess up the routine, or don't do it right, it just doesn't count, and I have to keep going.
Is the feeling that you need to check things multiple times driven more by the fear of what might happen if you don't, or by a feeling that you just can't move on until you've done it?

It's... well, it's kind of both, I think. I mean, I definitely get stuck like I was saying, where I just can't move on until I do the routine. But the reason I get stuck in the first place is this fear that something terrible is going to happen if I don't check. 

Like, even after I know I've cleaned my dressing supplies and the wound area, or even after I've reviewed a CAD file at work... this thought just keeps cutting in. It's like my brain is telling me that I missed one tiny thing, and because of that, it's going to turn into an infection, or a design mistake that actually hurts someone. And I can't just reason it away. I know logically I checked it, but the thought won't stop until I go through the routine again.
Is the anxiety you feel from not checking things multiple times more related to the fear of something bad happening or to the feeling that things are not in order?

I think it's definitely the fear of something bad happening, yeah. Like I was just saying a second ago, even after I know I've cleaned the wound area, or reviewed a CAD file at work, that thought just keeps cutting in. It's this nagging idea that I missed one tiny thing, and that it's going to turn into a serious infection, or a design mistake that ends up actually hurting someone. 

So it's not really about things just being out of order or messy. It's that specific fear of causing harm, and I just can't reason it away, no matter how much logic I try to use.
Do you feel like your checking behaviors have to result in a specific number or pattern of checks to feel complete?

Yeah, it does. Like I mentioned earlier, that's really the main reason I'm here. I'm just losing so many hours to rechecking all these things—the door locks, my dressing supplies, the file dimensions and notes at work. It's not just doing it once or twice. I have to go through the routine enough times until that anxiety finally drops. If I don't hit that point, or if I don't do it the right amount of times, I just don't feel allowed to move on to whatever I need to do next.
Do you feel like the number of times you check something has to be a specific number, like an even or odd number, to feel right?

No, it's not really about a specific number, like it has to be three times or an even number or something like that. It's more about just doing it enough times until the anxiety finally drops. Like I said, I'm losing hours to rechecking my dressing supplies, the door locks, and all those file dimensions and revision notes at work. I just have to keep going through the routine over and over until it feels right, and I don't feel allowed to move on until that happens. It's not a set number, it's just... however long it takes for the feeling to pass.
Do you think the anxiety from not checking would decrease if you were certain that your initial action, like locking the door or reviewing a file, was correct?

No, I don't think it would. I mean, that's kind of the core of the problem. Like I mentioned before, even after I know I've cleaned the wound area properly, or I've thoroughly reviewed a CAD file at work and I know it's correct, that thought just keeps cutting in anyway. 

It's always this nagging idea that I missed one tiny thing, and that it's going to turn into a serious infection, or a design mistake that ends up actually hurting someone. Being certain in the moment doesn't stop the thought from coming back. I just can't reason it away, no matter how sure I was when I did it the first time.
Is your need to repeat these checks more about ensuring you didn't miss anything or about feeling mentally certain that everything is okay?

I think it's really about both, but they're tied together. Like I was saying, even when I know I've cleaned the wound area perfectly, or I've gone over a CAD file and I know for a fact it's correct, I still don't feel mentally certain. 

That thought just keeps cutting in, telling me I missed one tiny thing. And if I missed that one tiny thing, it's going to turn into a massive infection, or a design flaw that actually hurts someone. So I guess the checking is to make sure I didn't miss anything, but the reason I feel like I might have missed something is because I just can't get that mental certainty. I can't just reason the thought away once it pops up.
Is the primary reason you repeat these checks because you fear something bad will happen if you don't, or because you need to feel absolutely sure everything is correct?

I think it's mostly about the fear that something bad will happen, but it kind of blends into needing to be sure. Like I said, I'm losing hours to rechecking things—my dressing supplies, the door locks, the file dimensions and revision notes at work. I don't feel allowed to move on until I've gone through the routine enough times that the anxiety drops. So I guess the checking is to stop the bad thing from happening, and I just have to keep doing it until I feel sure enough that the anxiety goes away.
Is the primary driver of your checking behaviors the fear of making a mistake that could lead to harm, or the need to feel mentally certain that everything is correct?

I guess it's really the fear of harm that drives it. Like I've mentioned, even when I know for a fact that I've cleaned a wound area properly, or I've thoroughly reviewed a CAD file at work, this thought just keeps cutting in. 

It's this constant nagging idea that I missed one tiny thing, and that small mistake is going to turn into a serious infection, or a design flaw that actually hurts someone. I just can't reason it away. So I check because I'm terrified of what will happen if I don't, not just because I want to feel certain.

patient.answer: No, it's not really about a specific number, like it has to be three times or an even number or something like that. It's more about just doing it enough times until the anxiety finally drops. Like I said, I'm losing hours to rechecking my dressing supplies, the door locks, and all those file dimensions and revision notes at work. I just have to keep going through the routine over and over until it feels right, and I don't feel allowed to move on until that happens. It's not a set number, it's just... however long it takes for the feeling to pass.

doctor.question: Do you think the anxiety from not checking would decrease if you were certain that your initial action, like locking the door or reviewing a file, was correct?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: Even after I know I’ve cleaned the wound area or reviewed a CAD file, a thought keeps cutting in that I missed one tiny thing and it’s going to turn into an infection or a design mistake that hurts someone, and I can’t just reason it away.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the nature of the anxiety and whether certainty about an action would decrease it. This relates to the persistent, intrusive thoughts (obsessions) that the patient has about missing a tiny thing and causing harm, despite knowing they've done the action correctly.

patient.answer:
No, I don't think it would. I mean, that's kind of the core of the problem. Like I mentioned before, even after I know I've cleaned the wound area properly, or I've thoroughly reviewed a CAD file at work and I know it's correct, that thought just keeps cutting in anyway. 

It's always this nagging idea that I missed one tiny thing, and that it's going to turn into a serious infection, or a design mistake that ends up actually hurting someone. Being certain in the moment doesn't stop the thought from coming back. I just can't reason it away, no matter how sure I was when I did it the first time.

target_item.name: Obsessions

patient.answer:
I think it's really about both, but they're tied together. Like I was saying, even when I know I've cleaned the wound area perfectly, or I've gone over a CAD file and I know for a fact it's correct, I still don't feel mentally certain. 

That thought just keeps cutting in, telling me I missed one tiny thing. And if I missed that one tiny thing, it's going to turn into a massive infection, or a design flaw that actually hurts someone. So I guess the checking is to make sure I didn't miss anything, but the reason I feel like I might have missed something is because I just can't get that mental certainty. I can't just reason the thought away once it pops up.

patient.answer:
